segments.he: רבינו ז"ל ראה פ"א בני הנעורים שלמדו הרבה אמר להם אם הייתם מקורבים אלי הייתם לומדים רק מעט אבל יותר "ווען איר זענט ציא מיר מקורב וואלט איהר ווינציגער גלערינט אבער שמתיר מלערינט". (כי היו לומדים לשמה ובקדושה וטהרה וביראה והיו עושים מתורות תפילות) וכמו שהי' אצל הרב הצדיק מבארדיטשוב ז"ל שחותנו אמר לו שמיום שנעשה חסיד לומד מעט מקודם. ענה ואמר לו מקודם הי' צריך ללמוד מעט עבור חותנו מעט עבור חמותו מעט עבור אשתו ומעט עכ"פ עבור השי"ת ג"כ וע"כ הי' צריך ללמוד הרבה כדי שיספיק לכולם אבל עכשיו שלומד רק בשביל השי"ת וכו' ע"כ כמה שלומד מספיק אחר בשביל זה אחר מקודם שהי' למד הרבה.
segments.en:
During the time of the height of the great controversy against Moharan'as — when the opponents issued a decree to destroy, kill, and annihilate all our fellowship — our fellowship suffered terribly, and it was a great miracle that all our fellowship were not killed then. A little of this is described in the letters of those years and in Yemei HaTela'os. And throughout that winter Moharan'as remained in Uman, afraid to return to Breslov lest they kill him. He was lodged at his companion Reb Naftali's home. Every day he went to Rabbainu's grave and prayed there for several hours. When he returned to Reb Naftali's home, he would ask for his letters [for his letters came to Reb Naftali's address]. When he read them he would say: "It seems I cannot yet return home" — for he could see from the letters that the controversy was still blazing stronger each time.

Once — after Purim that year — the ruffians on Purim broke all the windows of the Breslov kloiz in Uman, through the incitement and instigation of the Rabbi of Savran in Uman: "If everyone took one brick, nothing would remain of the kloiz." And they nearly destroyed the kloiz entirely — were it not for the fear that fell upon them from the distinguished men of the city who supported our fellowship. And it goes without saying what satisfaction Moharan'as had from this Purim — seeing the windows and doors broken and the kloiz nearly entirely destroyed. Yet despite this he strengthened himself then to fulfill the joy of Purim, as is cited in his letters. And then on Erev Shabbos parshas Parah when he went to the bathhouse in Uman, the opponents fell upon him and burned his clothes. But Reb Meir Blechir was with him and brought him other clothes. And throughout that winter — even though the fellowship from all places and the Breslov fellowship and his family from there sent him urgent letters imploring him for G-d's sake not to return to Breslov because they would literally kill him — despite all this, he was strong within himself that he would return, only he would extend his stay in Uman a little longer in prayer at the holy grave. And always when he returned to Reb Naftali's home he said: "It seems I still cannot return home."

After Rosh Chodesh Nisan — after that Purim — he came once from the holy grave, having stayed there much longer than usual. When he came to Reb Naftali, Reb Naftali saw a new expression in his face — that he was not as on previous days. And Moharan'as told him: "It seems I can already return home." Then Reb Naftali gave him the letters that had arrived — and he read them and said he would look at nothing and would return home [for he recognized from his prayer at the holy grave that it had been accepted and he could return]. And so it was — he returned home before Pesach. And the opponents gnashed their teeth at him — but the fear of G-d fell upon them and they did not touch him, for they had already seen some miracles by then.

But despite this, they succeeded with the government to station soldiers at his home who went through his house even on Shabbos — and this continued until Erev Pesach at midday, when they were taken back through the efforts of our fellowship. And on the night of Pesach when he went out in the morning, they found that the entire outside of Moharan'as's house had been painted with crosses — top and bottom — which the opponents had painted on all his walls. And yet the wicked were like a turbulent sea that could not be quieted — for they were furious that Moharan'as had the audacity to return to his home and was not killed. Therefore they reached the decision among themselves: Reuven of Yartzis — the greatest among them, a great scholar and so forth — had a son-in-law in Beroshid named Pinchasil who was also a scholar and man of good family and greatly esteemed among them, and he had already taken it upon himself personally to kill Moharan'as. They decided that immediately on the first day of chol ha'mo'ed they would send Reuven of Yartzis a special wagon — through one of their ruffians — to bring his son-in-law Pinchasil from Beroshid to his father-in-law Reuven for the last days of Pesach. And through this, certainly the end of Moharan'as would come, G-d forbid.

Our fellowship, when they heard this, their hearts melted within them and they did not know what counsel to take — whether to tell Moharan'as or not. No one wanted to bring such news to Moharan'as. Only the righteous Idel daughter of Rabbainu — when she heard this — could not contain herself and ran immediately to Moharan'as's house. He was always in his upper room, closed and sealed there in the service of G-d — and she went up immediately. When Moharan'as saw her, he was greatly astonished that she came so early in the morning — for he also saw wondrous allusions in this, always looking at the allusions of each day. And now, first thing in the morning, his first sight was the seed of Rabbainu standing before him. He asked her what she wanted, and she told him in fear and trembling: "Do you not know that they have sent for Pinchasil?" He stood a moment as if stunned — and replied: "He will most likely not come." "Mestome vet er nit kumen." She said again: "But they have already sent a special wagon for him!" He replied again: "He will most likely not come." When she heard him say this several times, she was reassured and returned home.

The end of the matter was: the wagon-driver — who was the chief of their ruffians — came to Beroshid with his wagon and saw a funeral procession going by for Pinchasil himself — who had suddenly fallen ill and died, G-d preserve us. The driver-ruffian decided to wait — not wanting to hasten back with such news — and arranged to return on the night of the seventh day of Pesach so as not to be seen and not to cause a commotion. But he arrived precisely as people were coming out of the synagogues on the evening of the seventh day of Pesach — and there was great excitement that he had come on Yom Tov. And the opponents, when they heard what had happened — they had been waiting all day with their eyes straining toward the road — their faces and the face of their leader Akiva of Artzis turned like the bottom of a blackened pot. And from then on they were afraid to kill Moharan'as.
